extracted.intended_audience: students, readers, and writers of English literary character-sketches; editors and scholars preparing editions
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for writing or judging short literary character-sketches and for producing a scholarly edition of such works. Emphasises individualisation, concision, analytic depth, and appropriate editorial apparatus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Individualising power
rubrics_metrics.description: The character-writers differ to a remarkable extent in their individualising power -- some of them achieving a high degree of success. (Earle has an exceptional power of individualizing.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give each sketch distinctive, individuating traits so the reader recognises a real person (examples: 'the contemplative man', 'the grave divine', 'the modest man'). Avoid merely piling on generic traits; aim for details that make a type feel like an individual.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of deceptive generalities (Dolus latet in generalibus)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Dolus latet in generalibus" is a salutary warning: character-writers should beware of the snare of mere generality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer particular, observable actions and traits over vague, sweeping statements. Anti-pattern: sketching only a class of behaviour without particulars that make a person believable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Profundity of analysis without turning sketch into essay
rubrics_metrics.description: Earle's distinguishing mark is 'the profundity of the analysis that accompanies the sketch' — he lets us know not only what the person looks like, but why they are what they are, 'and all this without turning his sketch into an essay.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include causal hints or brief explanations of motive or background, but keep them tightly integrated into the sketch. Avoid extended disquisitions, sermons, or long theoretical expositions that overwhelm the portrait.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brevity and density (conciseness as a virtue)
rubrics_metrics.description: Brevity is praised: Earle is 'swift and sententious' and 'densus' (dense). 'Brevity is the soul of wit.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pack thought closely; prefer concise, pointed phrasing over loose narration. Scoring note: dense, memorable lines are valued. Anti-patterns: slack, verbose sketches or needless expansion of a single observation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freshness and contemporaneity of observation
rubrics_metrics.description: Earle's observation is 'penetrating' and 'always fresh' — many of his characters appear 'really people of our own day.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for observations that feel immediate and illuminating to contemporary readers; avoid merely antiquarian or archival flavor unless that is the explicit purpose. Use examples and particulars that reveal modern resonances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of affectation, archaism, and conceits
rubrics_metrics.description: Earle's style 'is not uniformly conspicuous for quaintness, or that there is much that can be called affectation' and his phrases are 'surprisingly free from conceits.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use natural, precise language rather than forced archaisms or rhetorical conceits. Anti-pattern: stylistic mannerisms that call attention to themselves and obscure the portrait.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral tone: severe critic vs cynic
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish severe moral criticism from mere cynicism: the critic 'reports distressing facts,' the cynic 'invents disgraceful fictions.' The preface rejects calling Earle 'cynical.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When exposing faults, remain truthful and proportionate; do not invent humiliating or libellous details to score points. Balance severity with humane understanding (Earle's sketches often show compassion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Precision and balance of phrase
rubrics_metrics.description: Earle's prose contains 'phrases that we should be well content to use to-day' and is noted for 'precision and balance.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Craft memorable, balanced sentences. Use well-chosen aphoristic lines where appropriate. Examples in the preface serve as models of crisp, quotable phrasing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate scope for the sketch form
rubrics_metrics.description: The character-sketch 'is naturally a thing of limited scope' and cannot achieve the finished portrait a novelist might produce through long connected actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work within the limits of the form: select a few telling moments or traits rather than attempting full biographical treatment. Anti-pattern: forcing novelistic breadth into a short sketch.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delicacy of organisation and exposition
rubrics_metrics.description: These studies 'require a peculiar delicacy of organisation in the observer, as well as a special gift of exposition.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arrange details and observations with subtle structure so the sketch unfolds naturally; exposition should clarify without overwhelming. Judges should look for thoughtful ordering and economy of presentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate use of satire and wit
rubrics_metrics.description: Earle's 'piercing severity of his wit is illustrated everywhere' but is balanced by sympathy; his wit can be 'deadly' toward impostors and scoundrels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Satire should be targeted and justified by observation. It is legitimate to use sharp humour to expose vice, but avoid cruelty or gratuitous mockery of the genuinely unfortunate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of sermonising and overlong moralising
rubrics_metrics.description: Other writers (e.g., Bishop Hall, Butler) are said to turn sketches into essays or sermons; Earle 'never takes the opportunity to draw us into an instructive disquisition.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep moral points implicit or brief; do not allow a didactic agenda to dominate the sketch. Anti-pattern: lengthy homiletic passages shoehorned into a portrait.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concise narrative manner preferred over loose quasi-narrative
rubrics_metrics.description: Theophrastus' 'concise narrative manner' and the 'looseness or the connexion in the quasi-narrative' can leave readers unsatisfied; Earle's tighter form is praised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer tight, suggestive snapshots to a string of disconnected conversational scraps. A well-wrought, concise scene often outperforms a loose sequence of anecdotes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeless applicability or universality
rubrics_metrics.description: Though picturesque of its age, Earle's book is seen as 'as instructive a moralist in the end of the nineteenth century as in the beginning of the seventeenth' — characters often apply across ages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for insights that transcend period detail where possible; show traits and motives that readers can recognise beyond historical costume. If historic detail is central, make it serve the universal observation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editor’s scholarly apparatus and fidelity (for reprints/editions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Dr. Bliss's edition is praised as 'scholarly, more adequate, more self-sufficing' — it includes elucidation of text, notes, and other material (collations, MS evidence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A good scholarly edition should collate manuscripts, record variants (e.g., Durham MS, 'Bright MS'), provide explanatory notes, appendices (testimonies, letters), and retain original spellings in documentary material where appropriate. Avoid unnecessary tampering; supply editorial judgement and transparent documentation of choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion and documentation of supplementary material
rubrics_metrics.description: The Supplementary Appendix prints the Durham MS material, other MS versions, testimonies, letters, and notes; the editor 'retained in this Appendix the spelling I found.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include relevant documentary evidence (manuscripts, letters, collation tables, testimonies) and state editorial practices (e.g., normalising or retaining original spelling) so scholars can trace editorial decisions. Examples of acceptable appendix contents are enumerated in the preface.
